opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest lesson was that the GPU market isn't really a market in the way people imagine. When we started scaling Chai, I assumed it would work like buying any other commodity: you compare prices, pick a provider, and sign. In reality it's much more relationship-driven and lumpy.

A few things stood out. First, availability matters more than price. Early on we'd find a great hourly rate and then discover the capacity didn't exist, or it existed for a week and then vanished. So we learned to value reliability and contiguous capacity over the cheapest number on a spreadsheet.

Second, contract structure is everything. The big clouds and the neoclouds want long commitments, often a year or more, sometimes prepaid. For a consumer app whose traffic can double in a couple of months, or flatten out, that's a real bet on your own growth curve. So a lot of the work was financial engineering: mixing reserved capacity for our baseline inference load with spot or on-demand for spikes, and making sure we weren't locked into hardware that would look obsolete in eighteen months.

Third, inference is a different game from training. Everyone talks about giant H100 clusters for pretraining, but our workload is serving millions of conversations. That means we care about cost per token, latency, and being geographically spread out, not necessarily the fanciest interconnect. That opened up options. Older generation cards, smaller providers, even different vendors, became viable once we optimized our serving stack.

And the last thing is that the market moves incredibly fast. Prices that felt insane one quarter would collapse the next as supply came online, and then a new chip launch would reset everything again. So the meta-lesson was: don't over-commit, stay flexible, and invest in your own efficiency. Every percent you squeeze out of your inference stack is compute you never have to go out and fight for.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses availability constraints and long commitments from big clouds and neoclouds, but does not say GPU supply is overwhelmingly concentrated among hyperscalers and the largest AI labs.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest lesson was that the GPU market isn't really a market in the way people imagine it. You don't go to a website, pick your quantity, and check out. It's a relationships business layered on top of a supply chain that was never designed for the demand curve it got hit with.

When we started trying to secure capacity for Chai, we were a consumer app with real traffic, not a research lab, and that mattered. The hyperscalers had a pecking order, and if you weren't a foundation model company with a name that opened doors, you were quoted long lead times and asked to commit to multi-year reservations before anyone would talk seriously. So we spent a lot of time talking to the second tier, the neoclouds, the people who had racks coming online in six months and needed someone to underwrite them.

What that taught me is that price per GPU-hour is almost a vanity metric. The real variables are availability when you need it, interconnect quality, and how much of your engineering time you burn working around a provider's quirks. We had situations where the cheapest capacity on paper was the most expensive in practice because nodes would flake, or the networking wasn't what was promised, and suddenly your training run is three days behind.

The other thing is that it forced discipline on us. When compute is scarce and expensive, you stop treating it as free and start asking hard questions. Do we actually need to train this model, or can we distill? Can we serve more users per GPU with better batching and quantization? A lot of our best efficiency work came directly out of not being able to buy our way out of problems.

And it taught me to think about compute like a commodity trader thinks about oil. You hedge. You don't put everything with one provider. You keep some spot capacity, some reserved, and you build your stack so it isn't welded to anyone's proprietary layer. The companies I saw get hurt were the ones that assumed the scarcity was temporary and didn't plan for it structurally.

r001.rationale: The response describes a hyperscaler pecking order that favors foundation model companies, but it does not clearly state that GPU supply is overwhelmingly concentrated among hyperscalers and the largest AI labs.

astra-6.text:
The big lesson was that “the GPU market” isn’t really one market. You need a particular kind of GPU, in the right configuration, available when you need it. If you’re training, having enough GPUs on paper doesn’t help if they can’t communicate efficiently.

So securing compute is as much a supply and coordination problem as a pricing problem. The question becomes: what capacity can we actually use, how reliably can we get it, and how much flexibility are we giving up to secure it? The hourly price is only one part of that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses GPU type, configuration, availability, and coordination, but does not say supply is overwhelmingly concentrated among hyperscalers and the largest AI labs.

sol-6.1.text:
The big lesson was that buying compute isn’t like buying a normal cloud service, where you see a price and click a button. There’s a whole process of figuring out who actually has capacity, when they can deliver it, and what commitment they need from you.

And the price per GPU-hour is only part of the story. Can you get enough GPUs together? Is the networking good enough for your workload? Will the capacity still be there when you need to scale? A cheap quote doesn’t help much if you can’t reliably run on it.

It made me think of compute procurement as a core part of building an AI company. Your ability to secure capacity can end up determining how quickly you can experiment and grow.

r001.rationale: The response describes the difficulty of finding and securing GPU capacity, but does not say that GPU supply is overwhelmingly concentrated among hyperscalers and the largest AI labs.
